Le 21 août 2026, ce sont 1000 cartons de 24 bidons d’huile moteur contrefaite de marque OLYMPIA, d’une valeur de 43,2 millions F CFA, ont été appréhendés par les éléments de la coordination nationale de lutte contre la fraude. « Cette contrebande touche au droit de propriété industrielle, engendre la concurrence déloyale et porte atteinte à la protection de marque de produit et de service. Cette contrefaçon est prévue et réprimée aux articles 49 et suivant de l’accord de Bangui révisé du 14 Décembre 2015, les articles 26, 27 et 28 du code des douanes et les articles 46, 72 et 96 de la loi 016-2017/AN du 27 Avril 2017 portant organisation de la concurrence au Burkina Faso », a fait savoir Mohamadi Compaoré. Il a révélé que le 21 août 2026 également, sur la RN6 (Ouagadougou-Léo), un camion qui tentait de s’introduire clandestinement dans la ville de Ouaga-dougou, avec à son bord 30 tonnes d’engrais, soit 600 sacs sans aucun document, d’une valeur de 18 millions F CFA, a été stoppé dans sa course. Pour le premier responsable de la CNLF, malgré le caractère dynamique de la fraude, la coordination parvient à se mettre dans la même dynamique, en témoigne les différentes saisies. Il a salué la parfaite intelligence entre la coordination nationale de lutte contre la fraude et les structures partenaires. « Cette synergie constitue donc un rempart indispensable pour assainir les marchés et protéger l’économie et préserver des vies humaines », a-t-il conclu. Yassimine Aminata OUARMA Fadila Yasmine LENGANE (Stagiaire)

items.title: Peace on paper, peril in practice: Why 2027’s elections remain at risk, by Dakuku Peterside
items.description: There is something reassuring about political rivals gathering beneath one roof to sign a common promise of peace. In a country where elections have too often been accompanied by intimidation, inflammatory rhetoric, and violence, the symbolism matters. It affirms that opponents are adversaries, not enemies, and that the pursuit of power must remain subordinate to the survival of the republic. That is why the National Peace Accord signed in Abuja on August 18, 2026, deserves to be welcomed. It commits political actors to peaceful, credible, free, and fair elections, rejects violence and hate speech, and calls for impartial electoral institutions and professional security agencies. But Nigeria must not mistake a declaration of good intentions for an architecture of credible elections. The greatest threat to 2027 may not be spectacular fraud or election-day violence. It may be the gradual tilting of the political field before voters reach polling units: an opposition rally denied a stadium, a campaign permit mysteriously delayed, billboard charges raised beyond reasonable reach, state media favouring incumbents, or security rules applied firmly to one party and leniently to another. Individually, such incidents may appear administrative. Collectively, they can alter the character of an election. Democracy may preserve the rituals of competition-candidates on ballots, rallies, polling stations, and counted votes-while steadily losing its substance. A level ballot cannot compensate for an uneven field. Fairness begins long before election day. It begins with who may campaign freely, who can access public facilities and media, and whether government respects the boundary between public office and partisan advantage. When participation depends on administrative discretion, democracy becomes a permission economy in which those controlling the state also shape the conditions under which they are challenged. The same applies to INEC. Constitutional independence means little if financial, operational, or political vulnerability weakens institutional autonomy. Delayed funding can become delayed logistics, and delayed logistics can become disenfranchisement. Administrative weakness may achieve what crude manipulation once required. The legal framework matters equally. Uncertainty over electronic transmission, collation, and evidence in election petitions deepens mistrust. When citizens cannot tell which records are decisive or whether disputed outcomes can be meaningfully challenged, confidence diminishes. Technology alone will not solve this problem. BVAS and IReV are important tools for accreditation and transparency, but systems can fail, networks can disappear, and records can be contested. Disinformation can exploit technical uncertainty faster than official explanations can restore confidence. Artificial intelligence compounds the risk. Deepfakes, fabricated audio, and manipulated images can be produced cheaply and distributed rapidly, confusing voters, inflaming divisions, and persuading citizens that participation is pointless. Election technology must therefore be resilient, auditable, and governed by unambiguous rules. Transparency is now democratic infrastructure. Security agencies face an equally important test. The Peace Accord rightly asks candidates to restrain their supporters, but restraint loses moral authority when enforcement is selective. If one rally receives protection while another faces disruption, or journalists and campaign workers fear association with certain candidates, democratic space contracts. Incumbency presents another challenge. Office naturally brings visibility, but danger begins when governing and campaigning become indistinguishable-when public advertising becomes partisan messaging, official trips become mobilisation platforms, or state programmes are timed for electoral advantage. Public office must never confer ownership of public resources. Political language requires similar discipline. Where ethnicity, religion, and region overlap with political identity, reckless rhetoric can turn ordinary competition into existential confrontation. Once voters believe an election concerns their community’s survival rather than competing programmes, defeat becomes harder to accept and compromise more difficult. The consequences of failure extend beyond declaring a winner. Repeatedly tilted elections deepen alienation, weaken institutions, increase political risk, and erode confidence in democracy itself. Nigeria must therefore move beyond election preparation to an architecture of electoral fairness. INEC must make preparedness transparent. Governments must guarantee equal campaign access and separate state functions from party activity. Security agencies must publish and enforce neutrality protocols. Political parties must discipline their supporters. Civil society and the media must monitor venue access, airtime, security conduct, campaign finance, and digital integrity. None of this diminishes the Peace Accord. It gives it meaning. Handshakes, signatures, and public promises matter, but peace cannot rest on goodwill alone. A peaceful election is not necessarily a credible one. Legitimacy comes from confidence that candidates were free to compete, citizens were free to choose, institutions acted independently, security agencies remained neutral, technology worked transparently, and the same rules applied to everyone. That is the real test before Nigeria in 2027: not simply whether politicians keep the peace, but whether institutions keep the field level. The Peace Accord has placed the promise on paper. The harder task is making it real, because democracy demands more than peaceful competition. It demands fair competition. The post Peace on paper, peril in practice: Why 2027’s elections remain at risk, by Dakuku Peterside appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The Nigerian dream: Is it still alive? By Ejiro Ofoye
items.description: There is a question that Nigerians do not ask often enough, perhaps because the answer frightens us. Is the Nigerian Dream still alive? Not the dream politicians describe at rallies. Not the Nigeria of campaign posters, television advertisements and carefully prepared speeches. I mean the ordinary Nigerian dream-the quiet hope of a father who wants his children to live better than he did; the hope of a young graduate that his certificate will lead to a decent job; the hope of a trader that her business will grow; the hope of a farmer that he can return safely from his farm; the hope of a worker that his salary will last beyond the first week of the month. For generations, Nigerians believed that if they worked hard, educated their children and remained determined, they could build a respectable life. That belief is being tested. The question we must ask as a nation is no longer whether Nigerians still dream. They certainly do. The more troubling question is whether Nigeria still provides enough opportunities for those dreams to become reality. Nigeria remains a country of enormous potential. We have a large and youthful population, vast agricultural opportunities, abundant natural resources, a vibrant entrepreneurial culture and a generation of young people competing successfully on the global stage. Yet potential is not prosperity. For millions of Nigerians, daily life has become a struggle to keep up with the rising cost of food, transportation, housing, electricity, healthcare and education. Recent reporting indicates that although Nigeria’s economic reforms have improved investor confidence and some macroeconomic indicators, the benefits have not yet translated into meaningful relief for many households. That contradiction deserves our attention. What does economic growth mean to a family that cannot afford three decent meals a day? What does a rising stock market mean to the young Nigerian who has never owned a single share? What does improved foreign investment mean to the graduate who has spent years searching for a decent job? These are not merely economic questions. They are questions about the Nigerian Dream itself. Nigeria’s economy is showing signs of greater stability. The International Monetary Fund projects real GDP growth of about 4.1 percent for 2026 and says recent reforms have strengthened macroeconomic stability and external buffers. These developments should be acknowledged. Nigeria cannot build a sustainable future without macroeconomic stability. Reforms that improve government finances, strengthen the foreign-exchange market, attract investment and encourage production are necessary. But economic statistics must ultimately serve human beings. A stable economy that does not improve household welfare cannot be the final destination. That is why the success of economic policy should not only be measured by investor confidence. It must also be measured by the confidence of ordinary Nigerians that tomorrow can genuinely be better than today. Perhaps nowhere is the crisis of confidence more visible than among Nigerian youths. Across the country, young people are asking themselves a difficult question: Should I build my future here or seek my future elsewhere? The phenomenon popularly known as “Japa” is more than a migration trend. It is a reflection of aspiration, frustration and the search for opportunity. We should not condemn Nigerians who leave in search of better opportunities. There is nothing unpatriotic about wanting a decent life. The problem begins when leaving becomes the preferred expression of hope. A country should not export its brightest young people because it cannot create enough space for their dreams at home. Yet, even in the middle of this crisis of confidence, Nigeria continues to produce extraordinary stories. Our young people are building technology companies, creating music that travels across continents, developing businesses from tiny rooms, competing in global professional fields and inventing solutions to problems that should have been solved by government. The Nigerian spirit has not disappeared. If anything, it has become more stubborn. But resilience should not become an excuse for governmental failure. We cannot continue telling Nigerians to be resilient when what they need is a functioning system. A young entrepreneur does not need another speech about resilience when the cost of credit is prohibitive. A manufacturer does not need another seminar on productivity when electricity remains unreliable. A farmer does not need a motivational message when insecurity prevents him from reaching his farm. A graduate does not need another certificate when there are no productive opportunities waiting for him. Consider electricity. Nigeria is talking about electric vehicles and a cleaner transportation future while the country’s electricity system remains severely inadequate. The country is delivering only a fraction of the power required by a population of more than 200 million people, leaving households and businesses heavily dependent on petrol and diesel generators. There is something almost poetic about that contradiction. We want electric cars, but many Nigerians cannot reliably power their homes. We want digital transformation, but businesses spend heavily generating their own electricity. We want industrialisation, but factories struggle with the cost of energy. We want to compete with the world, while many of our businesses first have to solve the basic problem of keeping the lights on. The Nigerian Dream cannot be powered by generators alone. And then there is security. What is the value of economic opportunity if people cannot safely enjoy it? When communities are attacked, farms abandoned, businesses disrupted and families displaced, insecurity becomes more than a security problem. It becomes an economic problem and, ultimately, a problem for the Nigerian Dream. A farmer cannot dream when he is afraid to enter his farm. A child cannot dream properly when school is unsafe. A business cannot grow when its owner fears kidnapping. A community cannot prosper when its people are constantly looking over their shoulders. Security is therefore not merely one item on the government’s agenda. Security is the foundation upon which every other national ambition rests. This is why the Nigerian Dream cannot be reduced to GDP. A country’s economy may grow while its people remain anxious. The stock market may rise while millions remain outside the capital market. Foreign investors may become more confident while ordinary citizens struggle to obtain affordable credit. This is the Nigeria of two realities. One Nigeria is attracting investors. Another Nigeria is borrowing to survive. One Nigeria is discussing billion-dollar investments. Another Nigeria is asking how to pay school fees. One Nigeria is celebrating economic indicators. Another Nigeria is counting the days until the next salary. Both are real. Our challenge is to make them one Nigeria. That is the real test of economic reform. Reform should not be judged only by whether government finances look healthier or whether investors are optimistic. Those things matter. But eventually, the question must reach the Nigerian home. Is life becoming better? Can a worker save? Can a young couple afford a home? Can a graduate find meaningful employment? Can a small business obtain affordable credit? Can a farmer produce without fear? Can a child receive quality education without the family entering crippling debt? Can a sick Nigerian receive treatment without selling everything the family owns? These are the questions that will determine whether the Nigerian Dream is alive. And as we approach another general election, these questions must become more important than political slogans. The 2027 election must not become another contest of who can make the loudest promises. It must become a referendum on ideas, competence, character and performance. Nigerians must ask every politician a simple question: What exactly will you do to make my life better? Not what will you say. Not what will you promise. What will you do? We have spent decades changing governments without sufficiently changing the conditions under which ordinary Nigerians live. Perhaps the time has come to change the way we measure leadership. A governor should not be judged primarily by the number of projects commissioned, but by the quality of life of the people. A minister should not be judged by the number of conferences attended, but by measurable improvements in the sector. A president should not be judged only by economic statistics, but by whether the citizen at the bottom of the economic ladder can look into the future without fear. Leadership is ultimately about human beings. And the Nigerian Dream is ultimately about human dignity. There is also a responsibility on citizens. We cannot demand a better Nigeria while celebrating corruption when it benefits us. We cannot condemn electoral malpractice and then sell our votes. We cannot demand good leadership while supporting leaders because of ethnicity, religion, political connections or immediate financial rewards. We cannot complain about the country and then abandon our responsibility to build it. Nation-building is not the exclusive responsibility of government. But government has the greater responsibility because government controls the institutions, policies and resources that determine the environment in which citizens live. The Nigerian Dream is therefore a shared responsibility-but leadership must lead. So, is the Nigerian Dream dead? No. But it is wounded. It is alive in the student who still believes education can change his life. It is alive in the entrepreneur who refuses to close her business. It is alive in the farmer who returns to his land after hardship. It is alive in the Nigerian doctor, engineer, lawyer, teacher, soldier, civil servant, artisan and professional who wakes up every morning and continues to serve. It is alive in the Nigerian in Lagos, Abuja, Kano, Enugu, Port Harcourt, Benin, Ibadan, Maiduguri, Warri and hundreds of smaller communities who still believe that this country can be better. The Nigerian Dream has survived military rule, economic crises, political instability, corruption, insecurity and years of disappointment. But survival is not enough. We must make the dream attainable again. We must build an economy where hard work is rewarded. We must create jobs rather than merely celebrate employment statistics. We must make electricity reliable enough for businesses to plan. We must secure our farms, roads and communities. We must reform education so that our young people are prepared not merely to look for jobs but to create value. We must strengthen institutions so that the rule of law is not dependent on who you know. We must make public office a place of service rather than a shortcut to private wealth. And we must build a political culture in which competence matters more than propaganda. Nigeria does not lack wealth. Nigeria does not lack talent. Nigeria does not lack ideas. Nigeria does not lack hardworking people. What Nigeria lacks is the consistent conversion of these advantages into shared prosperity. That is the unfinished business of our nation. The Nigerian Dream should never mean that every Nigerian must become rich. It should mean something more fundamental: that every Nigerian who works honestly should have a fair chance to live with dignity; that every child should have a reasonable opportunity to rise; that where you are born should not determine how far you can go; and that leaving Nigeria should be a choice-not an escape route from hopelessness. The dream is still alive. But it is asking something of us. It is asking for leadership with courage. It is asking for citizens with conscience. It is asking for institutions with integrity. It is asking for an economy that serves people, not merely numbers. And above all, it is asking whether we are prepared to stop speaking endlessly about Nigeria’s potential and finally begin delivering on it. Perhaps that is the most important question before us. Not whether Nigeria can become great. We already know she can. The question is whether we have the courage, discipline and leadership to make greatness possible. The Nigerian Dream is still alive. But Nigerians should no longer be asked merely to dream. They deserve the opportunity to live the dream. *Dr Ofoye writes from Lagos. The post The Nigerian dream: Is it still alive? By Ejiro Ofoye appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: FG releases 2026/2027 Unity Schools admission list
items.description: By Joseph Erunke, Abuja The Federal Government has released the 2026/2027 admission list for successful candidates offered admission into Junior Secondary School One (JSS1) of Federal Unity Colleges across the country. The admission release, approved by the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, marks the commencement of the admission process for candidates seeking entry into the nation’s Federal Unity Colleges for the new academic session. The Federal Ministry of Education, in a statement issued by its Director of Press and Public Relations, Folasade Boriowo, said the development was in line with the government’s commitment to ensuring a transparent, accessible and orderly admission process. According to the ministry, parents and guardians can now check the admission status of their children and wards through the Federal Ministry of Education’s admission portal or the notice board of the relevant Federal Unity College. It directed successful candidates to print their admission slips and proceed to the Federal Unity College indicated on the slips for confirmation and completion of admission formalities. The ministry specifically directed parents and guardians to access the admission status and print admission slips through the FME Posting Portal at https://fmeposting.com.ng/auth/login. It urged parents and guardians to check the admission status of their children and wards promptly and ensure that successful candidates report to their respective colleges as required. The minister congratulated all successful candidates on securing admission into the Federal Unity Colleges and urged them to approach their academic journey with diligence, discipline and a strong commitment to excellence. The Federal Unity Colleges are among the Federal Government’s key institutions for promoting quality secondary education while fostering national integration by bringing students from diverse parts of the country together. The release of the 2026/2027 admission list clears the way for successful candidates to commence the next stage of their secondary education in Unity Colleges nationwide. The post FG releases 2026/2027 Unity Schools admission list appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: US appeals court considers reassigning case from judge over AI use
items.description: A U.S. appeals court has asked to hear arguments over whether a lower court judge in Mississippi should be reassigned from a ​case after he issued an order containing errors stemming from the use ‌of AI. A 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Friday asked lawyers in the case to be prepared at an upcoming hearing to address whether it should be assigned ​to a different district judge, “especially in light of the use of ​AI by the district court.” U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate in Jackson, ⁠Mississippi, was one of two judges who admitted in response to an inquiry by ​U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley last year that members of their ​staff used AI to prepare court orders in unrelated cases that Grassley called “error-ridden.” Both judges said the decisions did not go through their chambers’ typical review processes before they were issued. Wingate did ​not immediately respond to a request for comment sent to his court staff ​on Monday. Lawyers for the state and for the plaintiffs, which include the Jackson Federation of ‌Teachers, ⁠did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Monday. Wingate issued a temporary restraining order in the case on July 20, 2025, blocking state officials from enforcing a ban on diversity, equity, and inclusion programs in state universities and public schools. He then replaced ​the order after ⁠lawyers for the state argued that it contained references to made-up material, incorrect plaintiffs and defendants, and other serious errors. He declined to ​give an explanation for the errors at the time. In an ​October letter to ⁠Grassley, Wingate said that a law clerk used AI tool Perplexity “as a foundational drafting assistant to synthesise publicly available information on the docket.” He said posting the ⁠draft decision “was ​a lapse in human oversight.” The state in ​the 5th Circuit appeal is challenging a preliminary injunction Wingate issued later in the case. The appeal ​is set for oral argument on August 31.

items.title: Lutte contre la désinformation : sensibiliser les internautes pour une utilisation responsable des réseaux sociaux
items.description: Le cadre provincial des personnes ressources du Sandbondtenga a organisé, le samedi 22 août 2026, à Kaya, une conférence publique sur la désinformation dans un contexte des réseaux sociaux et de l’intelligence artificielle. Modérée par le ministre chargé de la Santé, Robert Kargougou et son homologue de l’Enseignement secondaire, Moumouni Zoungrana, la conférence publique, animée par le président du Conseil supérieur de la communication (CSC), Louis Modeste Ouédraogo, a porté sur le thème : «Désinformation à l’ère des réseaux sociaux et de l’intelligence artificielle : comprendre, vérifier et agir pour préserver la paix et la cohésion sociale au Sandbondtenga ». Organisé, le samedi 22 août 2026, à Kaya, par le Cadre provincial des personnes ressources du Sandbondtenga (CPPRS) dont le président est le Dima de Boussouma, le Naaba Sigri, ce conclave marque la toute première activité de cette association dont les membres sont issus des 12 cantons du royaume de Boussouma. Selon le coordonnateur du CPPRS, Ismaël Sawadogo, l’organisation de cette conférence se justifie par les dérives constatées sur les Réseaux sociaux (RS) entrainant certaines interpellations par les services compétents et le contexte de guerre qui recommande une communication saine prônant la paix et la cohésion sociale. Le président de la cérémonie, le chef de canton de Mané, le Naaba Sinbdo, a transmis les salutations du Dima de Boussouma au Président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, pour les différentes actions menées au bénéficie des populations. Il a exhorté les filles et fils du Sandbondtenga à construire la Patrie. Pour le représentant du parrain de la conférence, M. Kargougou a salué l’initiative de cette activité qui vise à promouvoir la paix et la cohésion sociale au Sandbondtenga. Dans son exposé, le conférencier a indiqué que la communication est une arme à double tranchant, en ce sens qu’elle peut aider à construire la paix et la cohésion, à régler des problèmes, à résoudre des conflits, à cultiver l’entraide, la solidarité, à éveiller les consciences, bref, à bâtir une société de paix et de développement. Cependant, elle peut créer des troubles à l’ordre social, la division, attiser les conflits, déstabiliser les Etats ou les institutions publiques, désinformer, diffamer, dénigrer, etc., en un mot, la communication peut être utilisée pour désorienter une société dans le but de semer le chaos. C’est pourquoi, il a salué la pertinence du thème de cette conférence publique qui permettra d’aider les populations à mieux appréhender les phénomènes de désinformation, des discours de haine, leurs conséquences potentielles sur la société et les bons comportements, réflexes et les bonnes attitudes que les internautes doivent avoir face à ces phénomènes. Toute chose qui contribuera à promouvoir la paix, la cohésion et la sécurité. En définissant les concepts, Louis Modeste Ouédraogo a souligné que la désinformation désigne une fausse information créée, diffusée volontairement, dans l’intention de tromper, de nuire. Par contre, la mésinformation est une information fausse que l’on partage sans intention de nuire. Désinformer pour déstabiliser Les populations de Sandbondtenga ont été sensibilisées sur les conséquences négatives de la désinformation. " data-large-file="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2-29.jpeg" class="size-medium wp-image-168118" src="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2-29-300x200.jpeg" alt="" width="300" height="200" srcset="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2-29-300x200.jpeg 300w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2-29-768x512.jpeg 768w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2-29-630x420.jpeg 630w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2-29-150x100.jpeg 150w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2-29-696x464.jpeg 696w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2-29.jpeg 1000w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 300px) 100vw, 300px" /> Les populations de Sandbondtenga ont été sensibilisées sur les conséquences négatives de la désinformation. Quant à la malinformation, il s’agit d’une information vraie, mais sortie de son contexte, ou détournée pour nuire à une personne ou à un groupe. A l’entendre, l’Intelligence artificielle (IA) désigne un ensemble de techniques qui permettent à des systèmes d’informatique d’exécuter certaines tâches n’existant habituellement des capacités humaines. « On peut utiliser l’IA pour faire de la désinformation, mésinformation et malinformation. Elle amplifie la capacité de nuisance », a-t-il précisé. De l’avis du conférencier, un autre phénomène accompagne la désinformation : les discours de haine avec pour mêmes objectifs de troubler la paix, la cohésion sociale et de déstabiliser les institutions. Pour lui, les personnes malintentionnées s’appuient sur la liberté d’expression qui est un droit fondamental, pour faire de la désinformation ou des discours de haine. « Leur conférant la liberté d’expression comme droit fondamental, les gens pensent qu’ils ont le droit de tout dire, de dire ce qu’ils veulent, d’insulter les autres, de dénigrer, de manipuler et de diviser les gens. Non, la liberté d’expression est un droit humain fondamental, reconnu par la Constitution du Burkina, par d’autres textes, mais cela ne leur donne aucunement le droit de dénigrer, d’injurier, de diffamer ou de manipuler à travers la désinformation pour déstabiliser le pays », a insisté, M. Ouédraogo. En termes de conséquences, le conférencier a déclaré que la désinformation affecte la cohésion sociale, le vivre-ensemble, la tolérance religieuse, la dignité des personnes, l’ordre publique, la confiance entre l’autorité et les populations. De même, selon lui, elle exacerbe les discours d’intolérance religieuse, la défiance, le discrédit des autorités, les troubles, la panique, la haine et les divisions des communautés. « Politiquement, elle menace la stabilité d’un Etat pour créer un sentiment négatif contre les autorités ou un soulèvement populaire », a averti le président du CSC. Pour lutter contre la désinformation, des mécanismes ont été mis en place tels que l’existence du CSC, de la Brigade centrale de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (BCLCC). Ces structures forment, sensibilisent, préviennent et parfois sanctionnent pour une attitude responsable sur les RS. En termes de recommandations, le conférencier a exhorté les populations à vérifier les faits, à adopter une grande responsabilité, à faire preuve de bon sens dans l’utilisation des RS. « Nous ne devons pas approuver, relayer des informations douteuses. Evitez d’accuser une personne, une ethnie ou une communauté lorsqu’il s’agit des faits graves. Evitez les messages de haine et la stigmatisation. Construisez la paix, la cohésion sociale envers les autres. Signalez les faux messages sur les RS ou interpeller le CSC ou la BCLCC », a suggéré Louis Modeste Ouédraogo. items.title: Burkina Faso : Les groupes terroristes recourent à l'enrôlement de mineurs
items.description: Les groupes terroristes recourent de plus en plus à l'enrôlement de mineurs pour tenter de compenser les lourdes pertes qu'ils subissent face aux forces combattantes au Burkina Faso. C'est ce que rapporte l'Agence d'information du Burkina (AIB), ce lundi 24 août 2026. Selon l'AIB, des enfants parfois âgés de 10 à 14 ans sont recrutés, formés à la hâte et utilisés pour diverses missions, notamment comme guetteurs, espions, opérateurs radio ou combattants. Le recrutement s'appuie sur la vulnérabilité des enfants. Les groupes armés exploitent notamment leur naïveté, leur situation de précarité ou leur peur pour les enrôler, parfois par la ruse et parfois sous la contrainte. Le Groupe de soutien à l'islam et aux musulmans (GSIM) est notamment présenté comme particulièrement actif dans cette pratique. Les enfants peuvent être affectés à des missions de surveillance, de collecte d'informations ou de transmission de renseignements. Leur jeune âge peut permettre aux groupes armés de les faire circuler plus facilement dans certaines localités sans éveiller immédiatement les soupçons. Les conditions dans lesquelles ces enfants évoluent restent particulièrement difficiles. Les chefs terroristes, confrontés à des difficultés pour assurer leurs propres besoins, peinent à fournir une alimentation et des soins convenables aux mineurs enrôlés. Ils peuvent également les abandonner lorsqu'une opération des forces combattantes intervient, privilégiant leur propre fuite. Des opérations de démantèlement de bases terroristes ont ainsi permis aux forces armées burkinabè de récupérer plusieurs mineurs. Certains enfants, âgés de 10 à 14 ans, ont livré des témoignages faisant état des violences et des conditions difficiles auxquelles ils auraient été soumis. Au-delà de la lutte contre les groupes armés, le phénomène pose donc un important enjeu de protection de l'enfance. La récupération de ces mineurs par les forces combattantes ouvre la voie à leur mise à l'abri et à une prise en charge adaptée à leur situation. L'enrôlement de mineurs rappelle enfin la nécessité d'une vigilance accrue des familles et des communautés face aux stratégies de recrutement des groupes terroristes. La protection des enfants apparaît ainsi comme un enjeu indissociable de la reconquête et de la sécurisation des territoires. Lefaso.net Source : AIB

items.title: Ronds-points embellis: la vitrine d’un Burkina résilient
items.description: De simples points de passage, les ronds-points embellis sont devenus aujourd’hui des espaces de valorisation urbaine et des symboles d’un Burkina Faso qui se réinvente malgré les défis. Ces transformations qui ont pris de l’ampleur depuis mai 2024, donnent un nouveau visage à plusieurs espaces publics du pays, notamment à Ouagadougou. Les ronds-points au Burkina Faso. Des points de repère permettant aux usagers de s’orienter et de retrouver leur chemin dans les villes. Endroits autrefois délaissés, certains de ces espaces ont profondément changé de visage et de fonction. Grâce aux différents aménagements dans plusieurs villes du Burkina Faso, notamment à Ouagadougou, ces carrefours d’antan ordinaires deviennent progressivement des lieux d’expression, de valorisation de l’identité nationale et d’attraction pour les populations. Ils attirent les regards, éveillent la curiosité des habitants et des visiteurs et constituent désormais des lieux de rassemblement où de nombreux jeunes viennent immortaliser des moments à travers des photos. Micknam Francis Ouédraogo, est de ceux-là. Ce Ouagavillois estime que l’embellissement des ronds-points est une évolution importante dans la perception des espaces publics. Selon lui, ils sont devenus des cadres attractifs où les populations peuvent se retrouver et profiter de l’environnement. « Depuis que ces espaces ont connu un changement majeur, les habitants les perçoivent autrement. Certains visiteurs viennent pour faire des photos, tandis que d’autres, simplement pour profiter du cadre », déclare-t-il. La marque de la verdure Il dit être particulièrement marqué par la présence de la verdure et des éléments décoratifs qui donnent une nouvelle image aux ronds-points. « Tout, dans ces espaces m’impressionne. Au-delà de l’embellissement, c’est aussi le signe que notre cadre de vie bénéficie d’une attention particulière », souligne-t-il. Les week-ends, à partir de 16 heures, ces ronds-points connaissent une forte affluence. Hommes, femmes, jeunes et personnes de toutes catégories sociales s’y rendent pour une découverte. « Actuellement, quand tu passes, tu as envie de t’arrêter et de regarder », témoigne Nabangsida Tapsoba, un autre Ouagavillois. Pour lui, cette initiative contribue à valoriser l’image du Burkina Faso. « Cela honore vraiment notre pays, cela donne une belle image à notre pays », affirme-t-il. Au-delà de simples aménagements urbains, il y voit le symbole d’un Burkina Faso qui se reconstruit et qui aspire à un meilleur cadre de vie. Il invite ainsi les populations à fréquenter ces espaces afin d’encourager la poursuite des efforts dans le domaine de l’urbanisation. Le visiteur, Ram Soudré, explique son attachement à ces lieux : « Ce qui m’attire pour venir faire des photos ici, c’est qu’on a mis les moyens pour aménager les lieux. Les premiers responsables du pays ont investi pour rendre beau notre cadre de vie, il est donc normal que nous le mettions en valeur », indique-t-il. Selon lui, ces réalisations permettent également de changer la perception du pays. « Quand nous faisons les photos, certaines personnes peuvent même croire que ce n’est pas au Burkina, et pourtant c’est bien au Burkina », dit-il dans un large sourire. Une résilience nationale Ce rond-point réaménagé à Bobo-Dioulasso, illustre la volonté d’embellir la ville et d’offrir aux citoyens des espaces qui reflètent l’identité et la créativité burkinabè. Plus que de simples espaces embellis, les ronds-points traduisent la résilience d’un Burkina Faso qui, malgré les épreuves, continue de se réinventer et de valoriser son identité à travers des initiatives porteuses d’espoir. Assétou Zongo est étudiante en génie civil. Elle voit dans l’embellissement des espaces publics plus qu’une simple opération esthétique. Ces aménagements traduisent, selon elle, la capacité du Burkina Faso à poursuivre sa transformation malgré les difficultés liées notamment à la crise sécuritaire. A son avis, ils modifient les perceptions négatives associées au Burkina Faso et montrent que le pays des Hommes intègres reste engagé dans une dynamique de construction et de développement. « L’embellissement des ronds-points est une initiative cruciale, car, il permet de déconstruire certains stéréotypes selon lesquels notre pays ne pourrait pas avancer à cause de la guerre », confie-t-elle. Pour l’étudiante en génie civil, ces réalisations témoignent également de la volonté des Burkinabè de ne pas se laisser emporter par les épreuves, mais de continuer à valoriser leur cadre de vie. Au-delà de leur fonction décorative, les ronds-points embellis deviennent des lieux de rencontre et de rassemblement, particulièrement pour la jeunesse. Ils incarnent ainsi une dynamique de modernisation urbaine et reflètent l’image d’un Burkina Faso résilient, capable de poursuivre ses ambitions de développement tout en faisant face aux défis actuels. Aujourd’hui, ces ronds-points invitent les populations à venir les découvrir et à les valoriser par leur beauté. Les visiter et en prendre soin, c’est aussi une façon de montrer son attachement au Burkina Faso et de contribuer à préserver l’image d’une Nation fière de son identité. Ange BONTOGO (Stagiaire)

items.title: Trump bought shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June, financial disclosure shows
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump invested as much as $50,000 in Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June, ​according to a public financial disclosure, giving him a financial stake in a ‌major government contractor run by his former adviser. He bought between $15,001 and $50,000 worth of shares on June 23, according to a financial disclosure he signed on August 12, which was made public on August 22. The ​purchase was part of more than 1,000 stock trades the president made in June. SpaceX priced ​the biggest-ever U.S. IPO on June 12, valuing the space, satellite and ⁠AI provider at $1.77 trillion. In a statement to Reuters, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said that ​third-party financial institutions independently manage the president’s portfolio and replicate “recognised indexes, such as the Schwab ​1000.” “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle said in the ​statement. Trump’s investment in SpaceX adds a new financial link between the president and Musk’s rocket ​company at a time when the administration is making decisions that could affect the firm’s fortunes. SpaceX is ‌a ⁠U.S. military contractor, and often seeks approvals from federal agencies. Trump on Thursday directed his team to help drastically increase the number of U.S. commercial space launches. SpaceX is a dominant player in that sector. U.S. Small Business Administration leader and Trump cabinet member Kelly Loeffler earned millions from SpaceX’s ​IPO, Reuters previously reported . Loeffler ​first invested in xAI, ⁠Musk’s AI and social media firm that has since merged with SpaceX. She invested again after Trump nominated her to lead the SBA. Her ​first investment in xAI would have been worth between $7 million and $2.6 billion ​on the ⁠day of the IPO, depending on the exact amount she invested and the date she made it, said Franco Granda, analyst at data provider PitchBook. The second investment would have been worth ⁠between $2.2 ​million and $25.4 million that day, he said. Reuters could not ​immediately determine the precise amount of Trump’s investment because federal officials use ranges to declare the value of their ​assets on their financial disclosure forms.

items.title: MTN approves $375 million share buyback after profit rise
items.description: Mobile operator MTN Group said on Monday that its board had approved a 6 billion rand ($375 million) share buyback programme, as it reported a 21.3% rise in half-year adjusted profit and strong cash generation. CEO Ralph Mupita told journalists the buyback programme would begin on ​Monday. At 1005 GMT, MTN shares were up 4.61% at 201 rand. Africa’s biggest ⁠telecom operator, with more than 317 million customers across 19 markets, said adjusted headline earnings ​per share (HEPS) rose to 793 cents in the six months ended June 30 from 654 cents ​a year earlier. Reported HEPS, however, fell 5.8%, hit by a 3.9 billion rand non-cash impairment on its 49% stake in Irancell, reflecting Iran’s hyperinflation and the sharp depreciation of the rial. Foreign exchange losses in South Sudan ​also weighed on earnings. The impairment comes as MTN seeks to exit Iran, its last remaining ​operation in a broader withdrawal from the Middle East. The process has been complicated by U.S. sanctions, in ‌place since ⁠May 2018, which have also prevented the company from repatriating about 880 million rand in trapped dividends, Mupita said. “With the sanctions in place, we can’t put any money in and we can’t take any money out. But if the situation did change in a way where there ​was a removal of ​sanctions we would continue ⁠with executing our Middle East exit strategy,” he added. Outside Iran, MTN’s biggest market, Nigeria, along with Ghana and Uganda, helped lift service revenue 17.5% ​to 115.3 billion rand. Growth in South Africa was 1.5%. MTN said strong subscriber additions and growth in digital and fintech services also supported its performance. Core earnings rose 24.4% to 56 billion rand, while the EBITDA margin widened 3.1 percentage points to 47.1%. MTN said the remaining hurdles to its ⁠tower ​deal with IHS Towers are largely regulatory. It has received conditional approval ​from Nigeria’s competition regulator, which requires it to reduce its stake in the Nigerian business by up to 30% over ​time at market prices.

items.title: DSS, NIA to probe NFF over alleged sabotage of national interests
items.description: The Department of State Services, (DSS) and the Nigerian Intelligence Agency (NIA) are investigating intelligence reports that certain top officials of the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) are working with some foreign interests to undermine national security. A security source disclosed that the DSS and the NIA intercepted highly disturbing communication between the said NFF officials and some foreign nationals capable of causing security problems for Nigeria. Asked if the investigation was linked the N17bn intervention fund released for salaries and bonuses of players at the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF), the source responded that it was beyond that, stressing that issues of financial impropriety are handled by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC). Said the source, “It is true that President Bola Tinubu in 2024 approved N17 billion as a special intervention fund to help NFF clear outstanding payments owed to Nigeria’s national teams. However, that falls within the purview of the EFCC, not the DSS and NIA.” “The mandate of the DSS is on dealing with domestic threats to national security. The NIA deals with external threats. So, when you hear that the DSS and NIA are jointly investigating a matter, it has got to be very serious, especially when the persons involved are saddled with the responsibility of managing an important body like the NFF,” he stated. However, the NFF has recently come under the scrutiny of many football fans who regretted that football teams have suffered neglect over funding, resulting in Super Eagles missing consecutive FIFA World Cups, and the historic failure of the Super Falcons to qualify for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil. The Super Falcons lost 1-0 to Cameroon in the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) quarter-finals, which ended their title defense and missed automatic World Cup qualification, subsequently facing a playoff path involving South Africa. South Africa’s Banyana Banyana defeated Nigeria’s Super Falcons 2–1 in the Women’s World Cup qualification playoff. Nigeria has played in every single FIFA Women’s World Cup since the tournament began in 1991, making this the first time they failed to qualify. The executive committee of the NFF headed by Ibrahim Gusau is under intense pressure to resign following the spate of alleged hi failures and also following the resignation of more than half of its members. “That at least half of NFF executive have or are contemplating resignation, may not be unconnected with the fear of DSS and NIA probe, fuelling fears on the possibility of holding the NFF board election scheduled for September 27 in Lafia, Nasarawa State,” declared the insider. The post DSS, NIA to probe NFF over alleged sabotage of national interests appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghana gold buyers went weeks without funds, sources say
items.description: Artisanal gold marketing agency GoldBod has not provided funds ‌to its gold suppliers for as long as three weeks, forcing some operators to halt purchases or borrow to stay in business despite surging bullion prices , five industry sources told Reuters. “The last two weeks were terrible. You could spend a whole day waiting and not receive any funds,” a gold ​trader in Ghana’s Ashanti Region said last week. Another GoldBod-funded buyer in the Western Region said funds ​had not been received for about three weeks. The sources asked for anonymity because they were ⁠not authorised to speak publicly on the matter. GoldBod, which makes advance payments to licensed aggregators for gold purchases, said in a statement on Monday, that there was no funding shortfall and that funding is provided based on creditworthiness, security, and risk assessments. The state agency ​said its gold-purchasing operations remained fully funded and operational, and it rejected any suggestion the agency had abandoned or was unable to finance its statutory mandate. Kwaku Ohemeng Amoah, chief executive of the Chamber of Gold Buyers, said GoldBod’s move to fund the trade from its own ​balance sheet after decoupling from the Bank of Ghana may have contributed to the funding constraints, adding that buyers could ​seek supplementary financing themselves. GoldBod’s chief executive, Sammy Gyamfi, said at a press conference last week that GoldBod raised nearly $839 million in advances for purchases between March and May. GoldBod raised about $75 million through a foreign exchange auction to commercial banks on August 3 before pausing it for consultations with the central bank. Three banking executives said the Bank of Ghana viewed GoldBod’s auction programme as inconsistent with its operating framework and that both institutions were working to address the concerns. Ghana, Africa’s biggest gold producer , established GoldBod in 2025 ​with exclusive rights to buy, ​sell and export artisanal ⁠gold as part of efforts to curb smuggling and boost inflows of foreign currency . GoldBod purchases were funded initially by the Bank of Ghana and helped to boost Ghana’s economic recovery, but the ​IMF called for an end to central bank financing after losses linked to purchases. In ​its statement on ⁠Monday, GoldBod said it currently has two licensed aggregators operating under its trade-finance framework and introduced tighter controls from August 1, including due diligence requirements, trade-financing agreements and security guarantees, to strengthen risk management and protect public funds. The Bank of Ghana did not ⁠respond ​immediately to requests for comment. The banking executives said that fewer than five ​banks participated in GoldBod’s auction programme, adding that lenders were more comfortable when the central bank backstopped the arrangement.

items.title: AES: les députés confédéraux, au nombre de 45, installés lors de la 1ʳᵉ session des parlements de la Confédération AES à Niamey
items.description: AES-INSTALLATION-DEPUTES-CONFEDERAUX AES: les députés confédéraux, au nombre de 45, installés lors de la 1ʳᵉ session des parlements de la Confédération AES à Niamey Ouagadougou, 24 août 2026 (AIB)- Le Président de l’Assemblée Législative du Peuple du Burkina Faso, Dr Ousmane Bougouma, également président de la session inaugurale de la 1ʳᵉ session des parlements de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES), a officiellement installé, lundi à Niamey, les députés confédéraux de l’AES, au nombre de 45, soit 15 représentants pour chacun des trois pays membres. Les 45 députés sont issus des parlements du Burkina Faso, du Mali et du Niger, à raison de 15 députés par pays. Ils portent le titre de « député confédéral ». Ils se réunissent dans le cadre de sessions confédérales pour émettre des avis et délibérer sur les questions liées à la Confédération. Cette 1ʳᵉ session, qui se tient du 24 au 29 août 2026 à Niamey, vise à poser les bases d’une coopération parlementaire renforcée entre les trois États membres de la Confédération de l’AES. La cérémonie d’ouverture a également enregistré la participation des délégations des parlements frères du Tchad et du Togo. Les travaux de cette 1ʳᵉ session se sont poursuivis par l’ouverture des assises du parlement de la confédération de l'AES, présidées par le Premier ministre du Niger, Ali Mahaman Lamine Zeine, représentant le Président de la République, le Général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani. items.title: Nevada sues to block Trump administration’s Colorado River plan
items.description: Nevada sued the Trump administration on Monday to block its plans to slash water supplies from the drought-stricken Colorado River, saying the move could devastate the state and violate the laws governing the river. The Department of the Interior on Friday finalised its plan that included a 21% reduction in water ​from the river to California, Nevada and Arizona for two years starting in 2027. The ​cuts to the three so-called lower basin states could nearly double after 2028, a ⁠move that Arizona and Nevada have said would have huge consequences for their economies. The four so-called upper ​basin states — Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming — face no mandatory cuts under the new 10-year plan ​to manage the river that provides water to one in 10 Americans and generates power for 6 million people. The plan is up for review every two years and the states were unable to agree on how to share the water ​after more than three years of talks to replace a plan that expires this year. Upper basin states ​refused to take mandatory cuts to their water supply from the river, arguing they already face steep reductions due to ‌the ⁠decades-long drought in the western United States. The three lower basin states say all seven states that share the river must make cutbacks in water use. The lawsuit by Nevada, the Colorado River Commission of Nevada and the Southern Nevada Water Authority is the first to challenge the plan. It was filed in federal ​court in Las Vegas ​and named as defendants ⁠the Department of the Interior, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation and its commissioner, Aubrey Bettencourt. The Interior Department declined to comment and the Bureau ​of Reclamation did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit ​alleged the administration ⁠violated administrative law, environmental law and the group of treaties, agreements and court rulings known as the Law of the River. It said the administration did not comply with requirements to consider reasonable alternatives and foreseeable ⁠economic impacts, ​to fully respond to comments, or to adequately analyse mitigation ​measures. “Consequently, decision-makers and stakeholders are left to guess at how federal defendants interpret and apply the Law of the River, which all ​agree governs the proposed action,” the lawsuit said.

items.title: Tunisian hospital receives 19 bodies after migrant boat sinks
items.description: A hospital in the southern Tunisian city of Ben Guerdane has received at least 19 bodies of ​migrants recovered from the sea over the past two days, ‌the head of a migrant rights group said on Monday, following the sinking of a boat at the weekend. The sinking of the migrant boat, which carried ​seven members of the same family, sparked a wave ​of grief and anger triggering violent protests in the city ⁠on Sunday night. Protesters burned tyres and blocked roads, while police ​responded by firing tear gas to disperse the crowds. Protesters are demanding better living conditions and economic development, saying that a lack of opportunities and years of marginalisation are pushing young people to undertake dangerous sea crossings to Europe in search of a better life. It was not clear if all ​the bodies were from the boat that sank. Mostafa Abdelkebir, the head of the ‌Tunisian ⁠Observatory for Human Rights, told Reuters that genetic testing was being carried out to identify the bodies and determine how many of them had been aboard the boat, while searches continued for other ​people who may ​still be missing. Tunisia ⁠was once a major departure point for migrants crossing the Mediterranean, but departures have fallen sharply ​over the past two years amid a crackdown and ​tighter ⁠maritime controls, backed by European funding and modern border-monitoring equipment, particularly from Italy. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and dozens of other human rights ⁠and humanitarian ​groups said in a statement last ​month that the EU-Tunisia migration deal had fuelled and normalised serious abuses against migrants ​and asylum seekers in Tunisia.

items.title: Secteur minier : La CIMR franchit un cap en prenant le contrôle conjoint de la CMT
items.description: Un fonds de retraite peut-il devenir un acteur de premier plan dans la gouvernance d’une entreprise minière cotée ? La question s’impose à la lumière de la récente opération validée par le Conseil de la concurrence, qui consacre l’entrée de la Caisse interprofessionnelle marocaine de retraite (CIMR) dans une nouvelle phase de sa stratégie d’investissement. L’autorité de régulation a en effet autorisé une opération de concentration économique qui redessine l’actionnariat de la Compagnie Minière de Touissit (CMT), l’un des groupes historiques du secteur minier marocain. Par cette décision, la CIMR ne se contente plus d’un rôle d’actionnaire financier. Elle devient, aux côtés du groupe émirati Ayrad Group Limited , copropriétaire exerçant un contrôle conjoint sur une société cotée à la Bourse de Casablanca. Le 13 juillet 2026, la commission permanente du Conseil de la concurrence, présidée par Ahmed Rahhou, a donné son accord à cette opération de concentration économique. La décision porte sur la prise de contrôle conjoint de la CMT par Ayrad Group Limited et la CIMR, ouvrant ainsi la voie à son entrée en vigueur sur le plan juridique. Cette validation intervient plusieurs mois après les premières démarches réglementaires. Le 7 mai 2026, le Conseil de la concurrence avait publié un avis relatif à la notification de l’opération, mettant à la disposition du public un résumé des informations communiquées par les parties concernées. Le document identifiait les acquéreurs comme étant Ayrad Group Limited et la Caisse interprofessionnelle marocaine de retraite, tandis que la société visée était la Compagnie Minière de Touissit S.A. La nature de l’opération consistait en une prise de contrôle conjoint dans le secteur de l’industrie minière, plus particulièrement dans l’activité de production de concentrés de plomb et de zinc contenant de l’argent. L’opération s’inscrit dans un processus amorcé plusieurs mois auparavant. En mars 2026, le groupe Ayrad , basé aux Émirats arabes unis, avait acquis l’intégralité des participations détenues par le fonds OSEAD Fund dans le cadre d’une transaction évaluée à 130 millions de dollars. Cette acquisition avait permis au groupe de prendre indirectement le contrôle de 37,04 % du capital de la société minière marocaine, tout en mettant un terme à plusieurs contentieux judiciaires qui entouraient l’entreprise. La nouvelle architecture capitalistique prévoit désormais un partage du contrôle entre les deux investisseurs. Ayrad Group conservera une participation de 37,04 % dans le capital de la CMT, tandis que la CIMR renforcera sa présence en portant sa part de 14,41 % à 16,12 %. Cette évolution ouvre également une nouvelle séquence réglementaire. Elle prépare le terrain au lancement d’une offre publique d’achat obligatoire (OPA) portant sur le reste des actions de la CMT cotées en Bourse, sous réserve de l’obtention d’une autorisation supplémentaire de l’Autorité marocaine du marché des capitaux (AMMC). Au-delà de l’aspect strictement juridique, l’opération suscite l’intérêt des observateurs financiers en raison du rôle joué par la CIMR. Pourquoi un fonds de retraite décide-t-il de dépasser le statut d’investisseur minoritaire pour participer directement au contrôle d’une entreprise industrielle ? La réponse réside d’abord dans la nature des actifs concernés. Les fonds de retraite sont soumis à des engagements de long terme vis-à-vis de leurs affiliés et cherchent à faire coïncider leurs placements avec ces obligations futures. Dans cette perspective, le secteur minier présente plusieurs atouts : des flux de trésorerie potentiellement stables, une capacité de distribution de dividendes et une visibilité à long terme susceptible de soutenir les rendements nécessaires au financement des pensions. L’investissement dans les matières premières constitue également une forme de protection contre l’inflation. Les métaux exploités par la Compagnie Minière de Touissit – notamment le plomb, le zinc et l’argent – évoluent en fonction des cycles économiques mondiaux. Leur valorisation permet ainsi de préserver, dans une certaine mesure, le pouvoir d’achat des actifs détenus par le fonds de retraite. Le choix de la CIMR répond aussi à une logique de gouvernance. En devenant copropriétaire exerçant un contrôle conjoint, le fonds pourra participer plus directement aux décisions stratégiques de l’entreprise à travers les instances dirigeantes. Une telle implication est généralement perçue comme un moyen de renforcer les exigences en matière de transparence, de protection des actionnaires et de gestion rationnelle des ressources. Cette présence institutionnelle pourrait également contribuer à stabiliser l’actionnariat de la société. Pour les marchés financiers, l’association entre un investisseur industriel comme Ayrad Group et un fonds de retraite de premier plan constitue un signal de confiance. Elle est susceptible de réduire les risques opérationnels, d’attirer davantage d’investisseurs institutionnels et de limiter les mouvements spéculatifs pouvant affecter le titre. L’opération apparaît ainsi comme bien plus qu’un simple réaménagement du capital de la CMT. Elle illustre une évolution plus profonde du rôle des grands investisseurs institutionnels marocains, désormais davantage enclins à exercer une influence directe sur les entreprises dans lesquelles ils investissent. Pour la CIMR, cette prise de contrôle conjoint marque une étape supplémentaire dans une stratégie orientée vers un « investissement institutionnel actif », visant à mobiliser l’épargne nationale au profit de secteurs productifs jugés stratégiques. Une orientation qui accompagne, en filigrane, les ambitions de développement industriel et de souveraineté économique portées par le Maroc dans les activités extractives et minières. items.title: Benjamin Netanyahu affirme que l’Iran a tenté de tuer l’un de ses fils
items.description: Benjamin Netanyahu a accusé lundi l’Iran d’avoir tenté de tuer l’un de ses deux fils, sans préciser lequel ni fournir davantage de détails sur les circonstances de cette attaque présumée. Lors d’un entretien téléphonique avec la chaîne israélienne Channel 14, le Premier ministre israélien a déclaré : « L’Iran a pris pour cible l’un de mes fils. L’Iran a essayé de tuer un de mes fils. » Cette accusation intervient alors qu’Israël reste confronté à de fortes tensions sécuritaires avec l’Iran. Le chef du gouvernement israélien s’exprimait notamment au sujet d’informations selon lesquelles le Shin Bet, le service de sécurité intérieure israélien, aurait refusé d’accorder une protection rapprochée permanente à Gadi Eisenkot, ancien chef d’état-major et principal rival politique de Netanyahu à l’approche des élections législatives prévues le 27 octobre. Netanyahu s’est prononcé en faveur d’une protection permanente pour Eisenkot, estimant qu’elle ne constituait « pas un luxe ». « Sans cela, les Iraniens réussiront » , a-t-il déclaré. Benjamin Netanyahu est père de trois enfants, deux fils et une fille. Il n’a pas précisé lequel de ses fils aurait été visé par cette tentative présumée. Son fils aîné, Yair Netanyahu, 35 ans, séjourne depuis plusieurs années régulièrement aux États-Unis, notamment en Floride, où il bénéficierait de la protection du Shin Bet. Sa présence à Miami a déjà suscité des critiques en Israël concernant le coût de cette protection pour les contribuables, certains habitants de Floride ayant également exprimé leur inquiétude face au risque de voir la région devenir une cible. Peu après les déclarations de Netanyahu, le journaliste israélien Amit Segal a affirmé sur sa chaîne Telegram que la tentative d’assassinat présumée était connue depuis « des mois », mais qu’une interdiction de publication aurait empêché sa révélation jusqu’à présent. À ce stade, les autorités israéliennes n’ont fourni aucun détail permettant de vérifier publiquement les accusations formulées par Benjamin Netanyahu contre l’Iran. items.title: Oil drops more than $2 despite new US sanctions on Iran
items.description: Oil prices slipped more than $2 a barrel on Monday as investors ​took profits after recent gains and shrugged off new U.S. sanctions on Iran . Brent crude futures settled down $2.22, or ‌2.35%, to $92.17, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude fell $2.05 a barrel, down 2.35% at $85.01. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced an expansion of secondary sanctions it can impose on entities and countries that maintain business ties with Iran around the world as Washington significantly ratchets up economic pressure on Tehran ​with the war nearing its 6-month mark. This followed Trump’s threats of “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale” ​against Tehran last week. “There is not much new that came out of Bessent’s commentary, beyond what ⁠was telegraphed in advance,” said Raymond James Investment Strategy Analyst Pavel Molchanov. The oil market having rallied quite a bit last ​week, saw profit taking today, he added. Both contracts posted a second consecutive weekly gain last week, rising more than 5%. “Can the ​White House come up with something that has never been tried before and will have a much more powerful effect on the Iranian economy? We’ll believe it when we see it,” Molchanov said. “The real question now is how aggressively Washington is prepared to enforce secondary sanctions against Iran’s ​remaining trading partners,” Jorge Leon, head of geopolitical analysis at Rystad Energy. “Unless China materially reduces purchases further, the additional impact on ​Iranian oil revenues could be relatively limited,” he added. Iran had condemned U.S. plans to announce new sanctions and President Masoud Pezeshkian had called ‌for a diplomatic ⁠solution . Pakistan’s army chief was visiting Tehran on Monday for mediation talks, ahead of the U.S. announcement. Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that once carried a fifth of global supplies, remained constrained. Fewer than 20 commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz at the weekend, shipping data showed on Monday, as Iranian and U.S. blockades restrict traffic through the chokepoint for energy shipments. TotalEnergies ​Chief Executive Patrick Pouyanne said the ​oil company was profitably ⁠moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz, with higher transport costs more than offset by steep discounts from crude producers. Iraq’s SOMO and QatarEnergy both offered crude for loading inside the strait in tenders, ​traders said. “$93 per barrel Brent, rather than $120-150, is telling us that enough oil is flowing ​through the Strait ⁠of Hormuz and from the Persian Gulf in general,” SEB analyst Bjarne Schieldrop told Reuters, adding that a turning point could be if Iran decided to actually close Hormuz with rockets and drones. Morgan Stanley analysts have increased their Brent forecasts, projecting a peak of $100 per ⁠barrel in ​the fourth quarter. The International Energy Agency is not currently discussing a second release of oil from its strategic reserves, its chief, Fatih Birol, said on Monday.

items.title: Dangote refinery drives seven-fold rise in Nigeria petroleum product exports, EIA says
items.description: Seaborne petroleum product exports from Nigeria have grown sevenfold since 2023, as output from the Dangote refinery improved regional fuel trade ​flows and boosted supplies to Europe and Africa, the U.S. ‌Energy Information Administration said on Monday. Here are more details: Seaborne petroleum product shipments from Nigeria averaged 561,000 barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, compared ​with an annual average of 79,000 bpd in 2023, Vortexa ​data showed. Of those shipments 350,000 bpd were exported during that ⁠period, compared with an annual average of 46,000 bpd in 2023. Dangote ​Group’s Dangote Petroleum Refinery, located in the Lekki Free Zone near ​Lagos, began operations in 2024 and is the country’s largest refinery. With the increased supply of petroleum products in Nigeria from the country’s largest refinery, imports fell, exports ​increased, and Nigeria became more self-sufficient in refined petroleum products, EIA ​said. Product shipments expanded after operations at Dangote began and again following the completion of maintenance and expansion in February 2026, coinciding with supply constraints at the Strait of Hormuz, EIA added. The maintenance increased the facility’s crude oil distillation capacity from 650,000 bpd to 700,000 bpd. Intra-Nigerian shipments rose to 211,000 ​bpd in the ​second quarter ⁠of 2026, up from 81,000 bpd in 2025 and 33,000 bpd in 2023. Nigeria’s seaborne petroleum product exports to ​Europe rose to 130,000 bpd in the second ​quarter of ⁠2026 from 40,000 bpd in 2025 and 15,000 bpd in 2023, while exports to Africa climbed to nearly 120,000 bpd from 89,000 bpd a ⁠year ​earlier. Nigeria imported nearly 400,000 bpd of petroleum ​products in 2023, and seaborne imports fell to less than 130,000 bpd in the second ​quarter of 2026.

items.title: Zambia closes courts on last day to file election challenge
items.description: Zambian authorities closed the country’s top courts on ​Monday, blocking access to the premises on the last day that ‌the opposition could file a challenge to this month’s disputed election. A memorandum from the chief administrator of the judiciary, which Reuters saw, said that “for security reasons, all members of ​staff are advised not to report for work today”. Police spokesman Godfrey ​Chilabi told Reuters that security assessments were ongoing and declined to ⁠give details. A spokesperson for the judiciary could not be reached. Opposition leader Brian ​Mundubile said last week that he was planning to file a petition at the ​Constitutional Court to challenge the results of an August 13 election in which he came second to President Hakainde Hichilema . The deadline to file such a challenge is seven days after the result was ​announced, which would be in the early hours of Tuesday. OPPOSITION STILL AIMING TO ​FILE PETITION At the Supreme Court premises in Lusaka, which also includes the Constitutional Court, all ‌of the ⁠gates were closed and police could be seen inside. Hichilema won re-election with about 60% of the vote in the Southern African copper producer, but two reports by independent observers found indications that Hichilema’s vote count was inflated. Hichilema has denied any ​fraud. Following the arrests of ​several of his ⁠associates, Mundubile was summoned by police for questioning last week in connection with alleged national security threats, which he says are ​fabricated. Analysts and human rights lawyers said they suspected he might ​be prevented ⁠from filing his petition, though Hichilema’s party said that Mundubile was free to use the legal routes available to him. “We are trying our best to ensure that the ⁠petition ​is filed, but we will see how it ​goes,” said New Heritage Party President Chishala Kateka, whose party belongs to Mundubile’s opposition alliance.

items.title: Trump Is Losing Touch With the Public
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. One of the few issues that unites voters and politicians of both parties right now is data centers. Three-quarters of Americans would oppose a data center being built near where they live, according to a new poll released last week by Heatmap Pro and Embold Research. The two leading lights of the left, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders, have sponsored a bill in Congress to create a temporary moratorium on new centers. They have an unlikely ally in archconservative Governor Greg Abbott of Texas, who said yesterday on ABC’s This Week that data-center companies “basically dug their own grave” and “got the backlash they deserve.” Standing against this consensus is Donald Trump. The president remains a big booster of data centers. “Communities that don’t take a data center—they’re making a mistake,” he said Thursday during an interview with his on-again, off-again lackey Michael Cohen. “Data centers throw off tremendous amounts of jobs and money.” This was no one-off. Trump had made several similar comments recently. “If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data center, I would absolutely want it, because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous,” Trump said last week—although he allowed that the sector could use “a little public-relations help.” This puts Trump, the most successful demagogue in American political history, in the unusual position of misreading, and opposing, a populist groundswell. During his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump took many stands that were unpopular among establishment politicians. Some of these positions put him at odds not only with Democrats but also with most Republican elected officials. Trump broke with Republicans in claiming that he would protect social-welfare programs such as Medicare and Social Security, and he broke a bipartisan consensus by attacking free-trade agreements and promising protectionism. On these matters (as well as on his willingness to encourage and participate in gutter racism ), Trump demonstrated that a big constituency existed for views that other politicians had deemed electoral liabilities. Data centers’ political arc has been different. Initially, many officials seemed to back the centers, following exactly Trump’s logic: They offered jobs and tax benefits. But as public opinion turned—driven by a mix of backlash to AI in general, environmental concerns, worries about energy prices, and old-fashioned NIMBYism— politicians changed their view as well . Why has Trump missed the shift? Presumably one reason is that he is surrounded by advisers and tech executives such as David Sacks and Larry Ellison , who are major boosters of and players in the industry. Tech companies invested heavily in Trump at the start of his second administration, lavishing him with gifts, including a gold-plated bauble and donations to projects such as his inauguration and his ballroom, and Trump has reciprocated by taking policy stances that benefit them. Trump may also be personally profiting from the AI boom; his financial disclosures show he’s become more of a tech investor . Trump has always tended to adopt the latest thing he’s heard, no matter what it is. He has been willing to alienate corporate interests in the past—when he saw some political upside. But he is not hearing from voters who might alert him to how unpopular data centers are. Trump’s rallies and speeches once created a feedback loop in which he conveyed his message to voters and—crucially—they conveyed their thoughts to him. Now, as his energy sinks, his travel schedule gets lighter, and security makes events more challenging, Trump is getting out less . Though his stump speeches dragged on for hours, Trump was carefully attuned to audience attention and what did and didn’t work. “You know, if it gets a little boring, if I see people starting to sort of, maybe thinking about leaving, I can sort of tell the audience, I just say, ‘We will build the wall!’ and they go nuts,” he told The New York Times in 2016. I think often about a speech Trump delivered in July 2022. It was billed as the launch of a new policy agenda, but as he read it, both Trump and his audience seemed bored. Then he ad-libbed a riff about trans athletes and the crowd came alive. Trump picked up on the shift and emphasized it; trans issues would become a central talking point for his 2024 campaign. The president has always been susceptible to fake news and bad at filtering information, but rallies provided a gut check about his base, if not about the broader national reality. Now Trump isn’t even receiving that kind of information. One of his major conduits for information is Natalie Harp , a sycophantic aide who isn’t interested in exposing Trump to criticism. He could read public-opinion data, but as his own approval sinks, he has taken to saying (and may well believe) that polls are fake. As his world shrinks, Trump’s populist touch has faded. Despite being elected twice on an antiwar platform, he’s launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. As the Iran war has gotten bogged down, he’s been incapable of reading the public mood. He has dismissed voter frustration over rising fuel costs, saying “I don’t even think about” gas; he previously called affordability a “hoax.” In response to reports that American sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln were struggling with a long deployment, Trump said they hadn’t been deployed “nearly long enough.” And the collapse of trade talks with Canada on Friday threaten Republican prospects in border states including Michigan and Ohio. Each of these cases represents a growing gap between Trump and his base, but none is as ironic as Trump’s stance on data centers. The AI facilities store terabytes of data, but the president can’t get access to the information about them that he needs. Related: The bubble-wrapped president Trump’s 2024 soft launch ( From 2022 ) Here are four new stories from The Atlantic : Sari Horwitz on the gun lobby’s most cynical move yet A reverse Ellis Island What a bicentennial baby knows David Frum on how to lose a trade war Today’s News The Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to move forward for now with plans to restrict mail-in voting , including directing the Postal Service to help determine which voters receive mail ballots. The ruling is preliminary and allows implementation to proceed while a lower court considers the legality of President Trump’s executive order. Trump said that the United States will impose 50 percent tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts, and steel beginning January 1, 2027. The announcement followed Canada’s decision to impose retaliatory tariffs on U.S. products after U.S.-Canada trade talks ended without an agreement over the weekend. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an “economic D-Day” for Iran, stating that the U.S. will impose new sanctions on more than 60 entities, individuals, and vessels tied to Iran’s nuclear and missile programs; additional sanctions are planned in the coming weeks. Dispatches The Wonder Reader : Isabel Fattal explores how relationships can change your personality . Explore all of our newsletters here. Evening Read From left: The comedians Anthony Atamanuik, Sarah Cooper, Alec Baldwin, and Brent Terhune Illustration by The Atlantic. Sources: Theo Wargo / Getty; Dimitrios Kambouris / Getty; @brentterhune / Instagram. The Trump Comedians Are Tired By Will Gottsegen In 2017, as Donald Trump was getting used to the White House furniture, Alec Baldwin was feeling exultant. His impersonation of the new president on Saturday Night Live had made him momentarily inescapable and given the comedy show its highest ratings in years. To capitalize on the momentum, Baldwin co-authored a book-length satirical memoir written from Trump’s perspective. Baldwin’s autobiography—which also came out that year and was excerpted as a cover story for Vanity Fair —noted that his take on the president “seemed to delight nearly everyone in the People’s Republic of Manhattan.” When he accepted an Emmy for his performance in the fall, he addressed Trump directly: “At long last, Mr. President, here is your Emmy.” It was disorienting, then, to hear Baldwin declare, when I spoke with him earlier this summer, that this sort of comedy has become stale, boring, and useless. “None of it’s funny. I don’t find it funny anymore,” he told me. “There’s nothing left to say about Trump.” Read the full article.
